abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel theoretical framework for understanding and predicting performance in heterogeneous supercomputing systems that integrate CPU, GPU, and specialized accelerators. Traditional performance models treat these architectures as separate entities, failing to capture the complex interactions between different computational units. We introduce the Unified Heterogeneous Performance Model (UHPM), which employs a multi-dimensional analytical approach incorporating data locality, memory bandwidth saturation, and workload allocation dynamics across heterogeneous resources. Our framework introduces the concept of computational momentum, representing the rate of change in effective throughput as workloads migrate between different accelerator types. The UHPM provides closed-form expressions for predicting optimal workload distribution in systems with dynamic resource availability. Mathematical analysis reveals fundamental limits on achievable speedup in heterogeneous environments, demonstrating that traditional speedup metrics underestimate true performance potential by up to 40% in real scientific computing applications. We validate our theoretical predictions through extensive simulation across 12 different heterogeneous configurations, achieving prediction accuracy within 8% of measured performance. This work establishes a new paradigm for heterogeneous system design, shifting from empirical optimization toward theoretically-grounded predictive design. The framework enables system architects to make informed decisions about hardware composition and scheduling policies before physical implementation, potentially reducing design iteration cycles by 60%. Our contributions fundamentally advance the theoretical understanding of heterogeneous computing and provide actionable insights for next-generation supercomputer architecture design.

Accurate performance analysis of parallel applications on many-core architectures requires models that capture the increasingly complex memory hierarchy behavior. Existing analytical models treat last-level cache behavior using simplified assumptions that fail to hold for modern processors with 100+ cores. This paper presents an enhanced memory bandwidth-aware performance model that significantly improves prediction accuracy for many-core systems. Our approach introduces a novel classification of memory access patterns into four categories based on spatial locality and access frequency, each exhibiting distinct cache residency characteristics. We develop a mathematical framework that computes effective memory bandwidth consumption as a function of core count, demonstrating that bandwidth saturation occurs non-linearly and follows a logarithmic growth pattern beyond 64 cores. The model incorporates contention factors that increase superlinearly with thread count, explaining the performance degradation observed in poorly-optimized many-core applications. We validate our model against benchmark applications including stencil computations, sparse matrix operations, and molecular dynamics simulations on three generations of Intel Xeon Phi processors. Results show prediction error reduced from 23% using state-of-the-art models to 5.8% using our approach. The model enables accurate performance prediction for applications scaling to thousands of threads, providing actionable guidance for thread affinity settings and memory allocation strategies. This work advances performance analysis methodology for many-core computing by providing more precise theoretical foundations that account for contemporary hardware characteristics.

This paper introduces Cascade, a novel distributed memory architecture that fundamentally rethinks data movement in large-scale supercomputing systems. Traditional cluster computing architectures treat network communication as a peripheral concern, implementing it through software layers that add significant latency and complexity. Cascade introduces hierarchical processing units with embedded communication capabilities, enabling computation and communication to occur simultaneously within the same physical operation. The architecture employs a three-tier design: compute tiles optimized for single-threaded performance, aggregation units that handle intra-node communication with minimal latency, and network switches integrated directly into the processing dies. This eliminates the traditional boundary between compute and network fabrics, creating a unified execution model where data flows naturally across the system hierarchy. We implement Cascade using custom ASICs with 64 compute cores and 8 integrated network ports per die, demonstrating 3.2x improvement in all-to-all communication patterns critical for scientific computing applications. The system achieves collective operation latency of 180 nanoseconds, compared to 2.3 microseconds in conventional InfiniBand systems at equivalent scale. For stencil-based PDE solvers representing canonical scientific computing workloads, Cascade achieves 2.8x speedup on weak scaling to 16,384 nodes. The architecture's power efficiency exceeds conventional designs by 40% when normalized for sustained application performance. This work establishes a new design paradigm for supercomputing systems, demonstrating that co-designing compute and communication elements from first principles enables transformative performance improvements.

We present an optimized runtime system for executing irregular scientific computing workloads on GPU-accelerated clusters that significantly improves upon existing approaches. Existing GPU computing frameworks handle irregular data access patterns through conservative scheduling that leaves GPU resources underutilized when processing sparse data structures. Our system, named AdaptiveGPU, introduces dynamic workload partitioning based on runtime analysis of memory access patterns, automatically adjusting thread block sizes and memory coalescing strategies for each kernel invocation. The key innovation lies in our lightweight profiling infrastructure that classifies workload characteristics within the first 10% of execution, enabling adaptive optimization for the remaining computation without application developer intervention. AdaptiveGPU incorporates a novel memory controller design that prioritizes access requests based on predicted future usage, reducing effective memory latency by 35% for sparse matrix operations. We implement the system as a drop-in replacement for CUDA applications, requiring no source code modifications. Evaluation on 15 representative sparse matrix computation kernels from scientific computing applications demonstrates average speedup of 2.4x compared to optimized CUDA implementations, with improvements ranging from 1.6x to 3.8x depending on data structure characteristics. For the numerical weather prediction workload tested, our system achieves 1.9x throughput improvement on a 64-node GPU cluster while maintaining strict IEEE floating-point compliance. The runtime system adds less than 2% overhead to application launch time, making it practical for production deployment in high-performance computing environments.
